gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a 65 W USB-C charge at 20 V needs 3.25 A, and that USB-C requires any cable carrying more than 3 A to be electronically marked. So with an ordinary unmarked 3 A cable, a 65 W travel charger can deliver at most 60 W (20 V × 3 A) to the laptop.
standout_why: I opened smartgadgetkit's UGREEN Nexode 65W travel review (cited) and best-batteries' Nexode 65W review (cited). They cover the 100–240 V input, the 45 + 20 W and 45 + 8.5 + 8.5 W splits, how the plug heads click in and release, the micro-cutouts with three devices, and 91.6 % efficiency. Neither says anything about cable current rating, e-markers or the 60 W ceiling of a 3 A cable. ChatGPT's own answers repeat the input range and the power split but never mention the cable. I scored it 2, not 3: I could not open a UGREEN page to confirm that the 90409 offers a 20 V 3.25 A step or that its box has no cable.
decides: It does not change the UGREEN Nexode 65W travel pick. It adds a condition to it: to get the full 65 W into a laptop, pair it with a 5 A (e-marked) USB-C cable. Otherwise the most the laptop can get is 60 W. It would favour a kit that ships with a 5 A cable, but I could not open any candidate page that rates its included cable.

findings.label: USB-C cables rated above 3 A must carry an electronic marker
findings.value: Cables are required to be electronically marked if full-featured and/or rated above 3 A
findings.source_title: SSZTBJ8 Technical article | TI.com (Brian Gosselin, Nate Enos)
findings.note: TI's wording: 'cables are required to be electronically marked if they are either full-featured and/or rated at more than 3A current.' On USB 2.0 Type-C cables: 'May be electronically marked (required if cable supports >3A)'.

findings.label: How the charger learns what the cable can carry
findings.value: An e-marked cable reports its characteristics to the charger over USB PD
findings.source_title: SSZTBJ8 Technical article | TI.com (Brian Gosselin, Nate Enos)
findings.note: TI's wording: 'Electronically marked cables use USB PD to provide the cable's characteristics.' Arithmetic: 65 W ÷ 20 V = 3.25 A, which is more than 3 A, so the full 65 W at 20 V needs an e-marked 5 A cable. On a 3 A cable the limit is 20 V × 3 A = 60 W.
